citation: Fanning J, Roberts S, Hillman CH, Mullen SP, Ritterband L, McAuley E. (2017). A smartphone “app”-delivered randomized factorial trial targeting physical activity in adults. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, 40(5), 712–729.
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; adoption/maintenance challenge [study rationale]
intervention: Smartphone self-monitoring app with tracking, feedback, and education; factorial add-on modules for goal setting and points-based feedback
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback; education; goal setting; points-based feedback/reinforcement
result_and_DOI: All groups increased MVPA by >11 min/day; points-based feedback was associated with higher MVPA and more favorable psychosocial/app-usage outcomes; goal-setting access was associated with higher app usage. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10865-017-9838-y
phase_structure: continuous 12-week active intervention; no separate maintenance or post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All four arms received the same basic smartphone self-monitoring app with tracking, feedback and education; factorial add-ons were in-app goal setting and/or points-based feedback
adaptation_or_personalization: none / fixed factorial modules — goal-setting and points-feedback access were assigned at baseline; no dynamic tailoring or response-adaptive sequencing reported
engagement_or_exposure: App usage was measured; access to goal setting was associated with higher app usage and points-based feedback with more favorable app-usage outcomes; specific exposure frequency NR in the current source record
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — behavioral effects were observed during the 12-week active intervention only

citation: Carr LJ, Dunsiger SI, Lewis B, Ciccolo JT, Hartman S, Bock B, Dominick G, Marcus BH. (2013). Randomized controlled trial testing an internet physical activity intervention for sedentary adults. Health Psychology, 32(3), 328–336.
population: Sedentary adults; N=53; enhanced Internet n=25, standard Internet n=28; mean age approximately 37 years
adherence_problem: Sedentary behavior / insufficient physical activity; adoption and maintenance over 6 months [study rationale]
intervention: Enhanced Step into Motion website with tailored motivational messages, PA tracking/logging calendar, pedometer-supported self-monitoring, goal setting, progress feedback, discussion forum/social support, exercise videos, geographic mapping, peer PA updates, and reminder emails
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; goal setting; feedback on progress; tailored motivational feedback; social support; observational learning/modeling; environmental support; prompts
outcome: Self-reported physical activity (7-day Physical Activity Recall; minutes/week); proportion meeting 150 min/week guideline
result_and_DOI: Enhanced Internet produced a greater increase in PA than standard Internet at 3 months (p=.03), but the between-group difference was not maintained at 6 months (p=.44). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028962
phase_structure: continuous 6-month active intervention with an intermediate 3-month assessment; no separate post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups received scheduled email prompts and internet access; standard-Internet control received links to six reputable public PA websites, while enhanced Internet added the theory-targeted website and tailored feedback/features
adaptation_or_personalization: static tailoring — monthly questionnaires generated stage-matched motivational feedback addressing individual barriers; tailoring was updated periodically but was not just-in-time
engagement_or_exposure: Enhanced-Internet participants averaged 18.3 logins in the first 3 months and 32.3 over 6 months; standard-Internet participants averaged 5.3 and 9.4 respectively; 22/25 enhanced and 26/28 standard participants completed the 6-month assessment
maintenance_interpretation: attenuation — the enhanced-Internet arm had an advantage at 3 months, but the between-group difference disappeared by 6 months as the standard-Internet group increased

citation: Zhou M, Fukuoka Y, Mintz Y, Goldberg K, Kaminsky P, Flowers E, Aswani A. (2018). Evaluating Machine Learning–Based Automated Personalized Daily Step Goals Delivered Through a Mobile Phone App: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 6(1), e28.
population: Adult university staff employees; N=64; mean age 41.1 ± 11.3 years; 83% female
adherence_problem: Fixed nonpersonalized step goals may discourage continued physical activity [study rationale]
intervention: CalFit smartphone app with real-time step monitoring and push notifications; intervention received automated personalized adaptive daily step goals generated from prior step/goal data; active control received fixed 10,000-step goals
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; personalized/adaptive goal setting; prompts/notifications; goal-attainment feedback
outcome: Objectively measured daily step count; step-goal attainment; secondary self-report measures
result_and_DOI: From run-in to 10 weeks, mean steps decreased in both groups, but the decrease was smaller with personalized adaptive goals (−390 vs −1350 steps/day); net between-group difference 960 steps/day (95% CI 90–1830; p=.03). DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/mhealth.9117
phase_structure: 1-week run-in followed by a 10-week active randomized intervention; no separate maintenance phase
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups used the CalFit app for real-time step monitoring, daily goal delivery by push notification and goal-attainment feedback; the incremental contrast was adaptive personalized goals versus a fixed 10,000-step goal
adaptation_or_personalization: dynamic algorithmic adaptation — personalized daily step goals were recalculated from prior step/goal history; this is adaptive goal personalization, not a JITAI or SMART treatment sequence
engagement_or_exposure: Frequent app use was reported for 17/34 intervention participants and 16/30 control participants, defined as app use in every consecutive 7-day period
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — the 10-week trial tested adaptive versus fixed goals during active exposure

citation: Slootmaker SM, Chinapaw MJM, Schuit AJ, Seidell JC, van Mechelen W. (2009). Feasibility and Effectiveness of Online Physical Activity Advice Based on a Personal Activity Monitor: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 11(3), e27.
population: Dutch office workers; N=102 randomized; age 23–39 years; mean age 31.8 ± 3.5 years
target_behavior: Sedentary, light, moderate, vigorous, and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (minutes/week)
adherence_problem: Low physical activity and poor awareness of insufficient activity [study rationale]
intervention: Personal Activity Monitor (PAM) plus PAM COACH website with uploaded activity scores, personal goal setting, activity logs/graphs, individualized activity advice based on goals/preferences/barriers, motivational feedback, peer comparison, and self-monitoring
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback; goal setting; tailored advice; action planning through preferred activities; barrier-focused problem solving; social comparison
duration: 3 months; follow-up at 8 months (5 months post-intervention)
outcome: Self-reported sedentary, light, moderate, vigorous, and MVPA minutes/week; PA determinants; fitness; body composition; program use
result_and_DOI: No significant intervention effect on PA outcomes after 3 months or at 8-month follow-up; usage was moderate and tailored advice was often rated unappealing. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.1139
phase_structure: 3-month active intervention followed by a 5-month post-intervention period with follow-up at month 8
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups were advised to increase PA; control received a single general PA-information brochure, while intervention received PAM monitoring plus PAM COACH tailored web advice
adaptation_or_personalization: static tailoring with progressive goals — goals were based on initial PAM score and personal target; advice used preferred activities and perceived barriers; goal scores increased progressively during the 3-month intervention
engagement_or_exposure: 73% reported wearing PAM regularly/often; 52% set a personal goal; 74% read tailored advice; website use varied across months
maintenance_interpretation: no maintenance advantage — no significant PA effect was present after the 3-month intervention or at the 8-month follow-up

citation: Hurling R, Catt M, De Boni M, Fairley BW, Hurst T, Murray P, Richardson A, Sodhi JS. (2007). Using Internet and Mobile Phone Technology to Deliver an Automated Physical Activity Program: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 9(2), e7.
population: Healthy adults; N=77; mean age 40.4 ± 7.6 years; mean BMI 26.3 ± 3.4 kg/m²
target_behavior: Moderate physical activity; leisure-time physical activity
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; barriers to initiating and maintaining planned exercise [study rationale]
intervention: 9-week automated Internet and mobile phone program with wrist-worn accelerometer; real-time web feedback, tailored barrier solutions, weekly exercise scheduling, mobile/email reminders, message board/social interaction, and activity feedback; control received accelerometer monitoring without program support
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; real-time feedback; tailored barrier problem solving; action/exercise planning; prompts/reminders; social support; perceived-control/intention support
outcome: Accelerometer-measured moderate physical activity; self-reported leisure-time physical activity; perceived control; exercise intention/expectation
result_and_DOI: Intervention participants had higher moderate physical activity than controls by accelerometer (p=.02) and leisure-time self-report (p=.03); the reported accelerometer-measured between-group increase was 2 h 18 min/week. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.9.2.e7
phase_structure: 3-week baseline monitoring followed by a 9-week active intervention; no post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups wore activity monitors and received basic verbal advice; control received no web/mobile program feedback, while intervention received the automated internet/mobile behavior-change system
adaptation_or_personalization: static tailoring — barrier solutions and motivational tips were matched to reported barriers and current PA level; no response-adaptive sequencing
engagement_or_exposure: Intervention participants logged in about 2.9 times/week; weekly participation exceeded 85% during the first 4 weeks and plateaued around 75% during the final 5 weeks
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — elevated activity persisted during the 9-week active program, but there was no post-intervention maintenance phase

citation: Wang JB, Cadmus-Bertram LA, Natarajan L, White MM, Madanat H, Nichols JF, Ayala GX, Pierce JP. (2015). Wearable Sensor/Device (Fitbit One) and SMS Text-Messaging Prompts to Increase Physical Activity in Overweight and Obese Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Telemedicine and e-Health, 21(10), 782–792.
population: Overweight or obese adults below recommended PA levels; N=67; mean age 48.2 ± 11.7 years; 91% female
target_behavior: Daily steps; moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA); total physical activity
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity; maintaining engagement beyond an initial response [study rationale]
intervention: All participants used Fitbit One for self-monitoring with instant tracker feedback plus web/mobile-app summaries; intervention group additionally received three SMS physical-activity prompts per day for 6 weeks
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; immediate performance feedback; summary feedback; prompts/cues via SMS
outcome: Actigraph-measured steps, MVPA, and total PA at baseline and week 6; Fitbit-measured weekly steps and active minutes
result_and_DOI: No between-group difference in primary PA outcomes at 6 weeks. SMS produced a short-lived week-1 advantage (+1,266 steps and higher active minutes), but this effect did not persist; Fitbit-only participants showed a small within-group MVPA increase at week 6. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1089/tmj.2014.0176
phase_structure: baseline/run-in followed by a 6-week active intervention with week-6 assessment; no post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups used Fitbit One for 6 weeks, received a brief goal/motivation intervention and PA guideline materials; the incremental contrast was three SMS prompts per day
adaptation_or_personalization: static preference-based delivery timing — participants selected preferred message times, but message content was automated rather than dynamically personalized
engagement_or_exposure: Intervention participants received three SMS prompts per day; about half judged this frequency too high, and qualitative responses indicated some stopped reading messages because they felt automated/impersonal
maintenance_interpretation: attenuation — an early week-1 SMS advantage did not persist through weeks 2–6 despite continued active exposure

citation: Gell NM, Wadsworth DD. (2015). The Use of Text Messaging to Promote Physical Activity in Working Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 12(6), 756–763.
population: Full-time working women; N=87; intervention n=41, control n=46; mean age approximately mid-to-late 40s
adherence_problem: Maintaining physical activity despite work, time, weather, and other common barriers [study rationale]
intervention: Approximately three targeted SMS messages per week for 24 weeks; messages were motivational, informational, and activity-specific, including guideline information, activity suggestions, goal setting, relapse prevention, social support, self-monitoring, time management, reinforcement, and barrier strategies; both groups received walking maps and website resources
BCT_or_mechanism: Prompts/cues; goal setting; relapse prevention; social support; self-monitoring; time management; reinforcement; barrier problem solving; informational/motivational support
outcome: Pedometer steps/day; exercise self-efficacy at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks
result_and_DOI: Intervention group had higher steps/day than control at 12 weeks (6540 vs 5685; p=.01), but not significantly at 24 weeks (6867.7 vs 6189.0; p=.06). Steps did not increase from baseline; the mid-intervention difference reflected a larger decline in controls, consistent with maintenance rather than absolute increase. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1123/jpah.2013-0144
phase_structure: continuous 24-week active intervention with midpoint assessment at 12 weeks; no post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All participants received workplace walking maps, website resources and PA guidance; the incremental intervention was approximately three SMS messages/week
adaptation_or_personalization: static targeted messaging — all intervention participants received the same core content and message frequency; content was adjusted for weather/seasonal events but was not individually tailored
engagement_or_exposure: 64 unique SMS messages were sent over the study; individual response to or reading of message content was not directly measured
maintenance_interpretation: attenuation / preserved behavior — the 12-week difference largely reflected less decline in the intervention group, and the between-group difference was no longer significant at 24 weeks

citation: Maddison R, Pfaeffli L, Whittaker R, Stewart R, Kerr A, Jiang Y, Kira G, Leung W, Dalleck L, Carter K, Rawstorn J. (2015). A mobile phone intervention increases physical activity in people with cardiovascular disease: Results from the HEART randomized controlled trial. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 22(6), 701–709.
population: Adults with clinically stable ischaemic heart disease; N=171; intervention n=85, usual care n=86; age ≥18 years
target_behavior: Leisure-time physical activity; walking; prescribed aerobic exercise
adherence_problem: Low participation/adherence in exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation due to psychological, physical, and access barriers [study rationale]
intervention: 24-week personalized automated mHealth cardiac-rehabilitation program: SMS exercise prescriptions and behavior-change messages plus secure website with video messages, progress tracking, goal setting, barrier identification/solutions, exercise tips, role models, and personalized feedback; intervention participants also received a pedometer; control received usual cardiac-rehabilitation care
BCT_or_mechanism: Personalized exercise prescription; goal setting; self-monitoring; feedback on progress; action scheduling; barrier problem solving; prompts/messages; role modeling; social support; self-efficacy support
outcome: Peak VO2; self-reported leisure-time physical activity and walking; self-efficacy; quality of life
result_and_DOI: No between-group improvement in peak VO2 at 24 weeks, but leisure-time PA favored intervention by 110.2 min/week (p=.05) and walking by 151.4 min/week (p=.02); self-efficacy to be active also improved. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487314535076
phase_structure: continuous 24-week active intervention with baseline and 24-week assessment; no separate maintenance or post-intervention phase
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All participants could access usual community cardiac rehabilitation; intervention added the HEART mobile program to usual care, while control received usual care alone
adaptation_or_personalization: static personalization — the mobile package used personalized exercise prescriptions/feedback and tailored behavior-change messaging, but no response-adaptive sequencing or JITAI was reported
engagement_or_exposure: NR — the primary report available for this backfill did not provide a sufficiently specific intervention-exposure metric for the unified manifest
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — behavioral PA differences were assessed at the end of a 24-week active intervention; no later post-intervention maintenance assessment was reported

citation: Harries T, Eslambolchilar P, Rettie R, Stride C, Walton S, van Woerden HC. (2016). Effectiveness of a smartphone app in increasing physical activity amongst male adults: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Public Health, 16, 925.
population: Healthy male adults; N=165 randomized; age 18–40 years; 152 included in analysis
adherence_problem: Low motivation or awareness to increase everyday walking [study rationale]
intervention: Always-on smartphone app that continuously recorded steps; randomized to no feedback, personal step-count feedback, or personal plus social-comparison feedback against the group average; feedback included current/day/history displays and refreshed every 15 minutes
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; feedback on behavior; historical progress feedback; social comparison (social-feedback arm)
result_and_DOI: Both feedback arms had higher model-estimated step counts than no-feedback control (individual feedback +60%; social feedback +69%); social feedback was not significantly better than individual feedback, and the feedback effect did not significantly change over the 6-week trial. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3593-9
phase_structure: 2-week intended run-in followed by a 6-week active trial; run-in step data were unusable because of a technical malfunction; no post-intervention follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All groups carried identical study smartphones with an always-on step-recording app; control had no feedback, one arm received personal step feedback, and the third received personal plus social-comparison feedback
adaptation_or_personalization: none / fixed feedback assignment — feedback condition was assigned at baseline; no dynamic personalization, JITAI or response-adaptive sequencing
engagement_or_exposure: 161/165 participants completed the study and 152 were included in analysis; no participant was excluded for non-compliance; step data were captured automatically without requiring user activation
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — feedback effects were evaluated across the 6-week active trial only; sustained behavior after intervention was not tested

citation: Fukuoka Y, Haskell W, Lin F, Vittinghoff E. (2019). Short- and Long-term Effects of a Mobile Phone App in Conjunction With Brief In-Person Counseling on Physical Activity Among Physically Inactive Women: The mPED Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open, 2(5), e194281.
population: Community-dwelling physically inactive women; N=210; age 25–65 years; mean age 52.4 ± 11.0 years
adherence_problem: Insufficient physical activity plus maintenance of gains after an initial behavior-change phase [study rationale]
intervention: 3-month mPED program combining brief in-person counseling, mobile app, and accelerometer: individualized short- and long-term goals, education, barrier strategies, social support, relapse prevention, daily messages/video, activity diary, automated reminders, and weekly goals increased by 20%; during 6-month maintenance, the plus group continued app + accelerometer while the regular group continued accelerometer only
BCT_or_mechanism: Goal setting; self-monitoring; feedback; graded goals; barrier problem solving; social support; relapse prevention; prompts/reminders; education
result_and_DOI: During the first 3 months, the combined intervention groups increased activity versus control by 2,060 steps/day and 18.2 min/day MVPA. During the next 6 months, continuing the app did not provide a significant maintenance advantage over accelerometer-only maintenance. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2019.4281
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Control used an accelerometer for 9 months without intervention; regular and plus groups received identical app + counseling + accelerometer during acquisition; during maintenance both kept the accelerometer, while only plus retained the app and was encouraged to continue the physical-activity diary
adaptation_or_personalization: static individualized tailoring + automated graded goals — counseling set individualized goals from baseline data and weekly goals increased by 20% until 10,000 steps/day; no response-adaptive treatment sequencing
engagement_or_exposure: Initial 3-month adherence to daily messages/video and diary was about 85.5%–85.7%; maintenance-phase diary adherence in the plus group was 68.4%; counseling-session attendance was 94%–100%
maintenance_interpretation: no maintenance advantage — activity remained above control but declined at similar rates in regular and plus groups; continued app diary use did not improve maintenance versus accelerometer-only maintenance

citation: Simoes MDSMP, Proença NL, Lauria VT, do Nascimento MB, Padovani RDC, Dourado VZ. (2026). Effects of Using a Smartphone App Combined With Behavior Change Techniques on the Level of Physical Activity Among Adults and Older Adults: Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 28, e73388.
population: Adults and older adults; N=53; mean age 44.0 ± 12.7 years
adherence_problem: Physical-activity engagement declines over time; initial nonresponse may require treatment adaptation [study rationale]
intervention: Initial randomization to app + tailored messages, app + tailored messages + gamification I, or educational control; at week 6 intervention participants were classified as responders/nonresponders and nonresponders could receive an adapted second-stage package including gamification II; after week 12 participants were advised to continue app step monitoring without direct researcher intervention
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; individual goal setting; tailored messages/feedback; graded tasks; virtual badges/rewards; ranking/social comparison; social support; educational instruction
duration: 24 weeks total: 12-week active multistage intervention + 12-week follow-up
outcome: Accelerometer-measured daily steps, sedentary behavior and MVPA
result_and_DOI: Group 1 increased daily steps across assessments and maintained gains at follow-up; responder trajectories were favorable; control step counts declined at follow-up. Do not attribute the result to gamification alone. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/73388
phase_structure: 0–6 weeks initial treatment → week-6 response classification → 6–12 weeks adapted second stage → 12–24 weeks self-directed follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Educational-information control; intervention arms share app-based monitoring but differ in tailored messages/gamification and response-triggered escalation
adaptation_or_personalization: Response-adaptive sequencing (SMART); treatment changes depend on week-6 step-count response
engagement_or_exposure: Groups 1 and 2 had 63% and 47% responders at week 6; only one participant explored unassigned app gamification features; follow-up continued app monitoring without direct researcher interference
maintenance_interpretation: sustained gain — favorable step-count trajectory persisted into follow-up for group 1/responders, while control declined

citation: Sagelv EH, Manskow US, Antypas K, Morseth B, Aksetøy ILA, Nes BM, Gagnon MP, Zanaboni P. (2025). Online interventions to increase physical activity levels in self-reported inactive adults: the ONWARDS randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine.
population: Self-reported inactive adults; N=183; age 22–55 years
target_behavior: MVPA; light PA; total PA; steps; sedentary time
adherence_problem: Long-term effectiveness and maintenance of digitally supported physical activity [study rationale]
intervention: Group A: activity tracker + PAI app; Group B: A + home-based online training; Group C: B + closed social-media peer support
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; personalized feedback via PAI; goal/reference metric; structured home exercise; peer/social support
duration: 18 months with assessments at 6, 12 and 18 months
outcome: ActiGraph-measured MVPA, light PA, total PA, steps and sedentary time
result_and_DOI: No sustained group-by-time advantage across the increasingly intensive packages; Group C showed a temporary 6-month MVPA advantage, then groups converged; overall MVPA declined over 18 months. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjsem-2023-001816
phase_structure: continuous 18-month exposure with long-term repeated follow-up
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All arms received tracker + PAI app; B added online training; C added online training + peer support; no inactive/no-intervention control
adaptation_or_personalization: Static personalization via PAI metric; no response-adaptive sequencing
engagement_or_exposure: Accelerometer follow-up completeness fell to 42.7% at 18 months; fully web-based delivery limited control over component use
maintenance_interpretation: attenuation — temporary early advantage from added peer-support layer did not persist; groups converged while overall MVPA declined

citation: Vos AL, de Bruijn GJ, Klein MCA, Boerman SC, Stuber JM, Smit EG. (2025). Effectiveness of a Just-In-Time Adaptive App to Increase Daily Steps: An RCT. American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 68(1).
population: Adults in low-socioeconomic-position neighborhoods in the Netherlands; N=176; mean age ≈56 years; 76% female
adherence_problem: Need for context-sensitive, individually relevant support to promote walking [study rationale]
intervention: Intervention: step-counter app + dynamically tailored just-in-time coaching delivered through push notifications; control: step-counter app only
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; individually tailored feedback; preference-sensitive walking advice; context-aware suggestions linked to suitable walking locations
duration: 6 or 12 months depending on municipality/funding period; questionnaires at 3, 6 and 12 months where applicable
result_and_DOI: No significant average intervention effect on steps over time; perceived usefulness significantly moderated the intervention effect, with more favorable response among participants reporting greater usefulness. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2024.09.010
phase_structure: continuous exposure with longitudinal follow-up; not a clean acquisition→maintenance design
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups received a step-counter/self-monitoring app; incremental contrast was the JITAI coaching layer
adaptation_or_personalization: Contextual/JITAI tailoring based on participant/context information and preferences
engagement_or_exposure: About 30% of possible daily step observations were present; missingness increased over time; actual reading of coaching messages could not be verified
maintenance_interpretation: no maintenance advantage — no average incremental step benefit over active self-monitoring control; experienced usefulness modified response

citation: Brickwood KJ, Ahuja KDK, Watson G, O'Brien J, Williams AD. (2021). Effects of Activity Tracker Use With Health Professional Support or Telephone Counseling on Maintenance of Physical Activity and Health Outcomes in Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 9(1), e18686.
population: Older adults >60 years; N=117; mean age 72.4 ± 6.4 years; participants had just completed a 12-week individualized community exercise program
target_behavior: Daily steps; nonstepping time; physical activity maintenance
adherence_problem: Maintaining physical activity after completion of a structured exercise program [study rationale]
intervention: Activity tracker + smartphone app + accredited exercise-physiologist support versus telephone counseling versus usual care
BCT_or_mechanism: Self-monitoring; goal setting; feedback; motivational interviewing / self-efficacy support
duration: 12 months with assessments at 3, 6 and 12 months
outcome: ActivPAL-measured daily steps and nonstepping time; Active Australia Survey self-report
result_and_DOI: Tracker and telephone-counseling groups broadly maintained daily steps while usual care declined; between-group differences were not uniformly significant. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/18686
phase_structure: post-program maintenance trial beginning immediately after a prior 12-week exercise intervention
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: All participants entered after the same prior community exercise program; randomized maintenance support was tracker+AEP versus telephone counseling versus usual care
adaptation_or_personalization: No adaptive sequencing; support was personalized/professional but not JITAI
engagement_or_exposure: Tracker group wore the device on about 84% of available days; telephone group received about 12 calls averaging 11.1 minutes
maintenance_interpretation: preserved behavior — tracker and telephone-support groups largely maintained steps rather than showing clear additional gains

citation: Yoshimura E, Tajiri E, Michiwaki R, Matsumoto N, Hatamoto Y, Tanaka S. (2022). Long-term Effects of the Use of a Step Count–Specific Smartphone App on Physical Activity and Weight Loss: Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 10(10), e35628.
population: Adults aged 30–60 years; N=109; mean age 47 ± 8 years
adherence_problem: Long-duration support for increasing physical activity during a weight-management program [study rationale]
intervention: App group used a step-count/ranking smartphone app; both groups received a 1-hour PA/weight-loss lecture, daily self-weighing instructions, monthly advisory emails and periodic feedback
BCT_or_mechanism: Step self-monitoring; group ranking/social comparison; goal setting (+1000 steps/day); shared education, self-weighing, motivational emails and feedback
outcome: Triaxial-accelerometer step count and MVPA; body weight measured separately
result_and_DOI: App group showed a more favorable step-count trajectory, especially on weekends; increased PA did not produce additional weight loss versus control. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/35628
phase_structure: continuous 32-week active exposure; not automatically a maintenance phase
shared_backbone_or_active_comparator: Both groups received lecture, self-weighing, monthly motivational emails and periodic feedback; incremental contrast was daily app step/rank checking
adaptation_or_personalization: No adaptive sequencing; static app-based self-monitoring/ranking
engagement_or_exposure: App checking at least daily was about 80.1% through 12 weeks and 73.6% during weeks 12–32; dropout at 32 weeks was low
maintenance_interpretation: not a maintenance design — long-duration active exposure showed PA benefit without additional weight-loss benefit
